title: Frontiers in Blood & Hemostasis
summary: Cutting-edge tools and therapies reshaping how we test clotting, save blood, and cure inherited blood disease.

lessons.title: Viscoelastic Testing: TEG & ROTEM-Guided Hemostasis

levels.kid:
Imagine making jelly. First it is runny. Then it slowly gets thick and wobbly. If you poke it, you can feel how strong it is.

Blood does something similar when you get a cut. It turns from a liquid into a soft, strong plug called a **clot**. That plug stops the bleeding.

Doctors have special machines that watch a tiny drop of blood turn into a clot. The machine gently wiggles the blood and feels how fast the clot forms, how strong it gets, and whether it falls apart too soon.

This helps doctors during big operations. If the clot is weak, they can give the exact missing piece, instead of guessing. It is like a cook tasting the soup before adding salt.
levels.hs:
When you bleed, your body builds a clot in steps. Proteins called **clotting factors** make threads of **fibrin**, and tiny cell pieces called **platelets** stick together and pull the threads tight. Later, a process called **fibrinolysis** breaks the clot down when it is no longer needed.

Standard lab tests, like the **PT** and **aPTT**, only measure how long plasma takes to start forming fibrin. They stop timing at the very first strands, and they leave out platelets and red cells.

**Viscoelastic tests** look at the whole clot instead. The two main ones are **TEG** (thromboelastography) and **ROTEM** (rotational thromboelastometry). A small sample of whole blood sits in a cup with a pin. As the clot forms, it connects the pin and cup. A sensor records how stiff the clot becomes over time and draws a curve.

The curve shows:
- **How fast** clotting starts (clotting factors)
- **How strong** the clot gets (mostly platelets and fibrinogen)
- **Whether it breaks down early** (too much fibrinolysis)

A real example: in a trauma patient bleeding heavily, the curve might show a weak clot because fibrinogen is low. The team can then give fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate, rather than pouring in every blood product. Results come in about 10 to 30 minutes, right at the bedside.
levels.college:
Viscoelastic hemostatic assays (VHAs) measure the mechanical properties of whole blood as it clots. This captures the cell-based model of coagulation, in which platelets, red cells and plasma factors work together. Conventional plasma tests (PT/INR, aPTT) only report time to the first fibrin formation.

**How they work.** In classic **TEG**, the cup oscillates and the clot transmits torque to a suspended pin. In **ROTEM**, the pin rotates and the cup is still. Newer devices, such as **TEG 6s** and **Quantra**, use resonance or ultrasound in cartridges. Each device produces a trace of clot firmness over time.

**Key parameters (TEG / ROTEM names):**
- **R / CT** (reaction time / clotting time): time to initial fibrin. Prolonged with factor deficiency or heparin. Treated with plasma or prothrombin complex concentrate.
- **K and alpha angle / CFT**: speed of clot build-up. Reflects fibrinogen and thrombin generation.
- **MA / MCF** (maximum amplitude / maximum clot firmness): peak strength. Platelets contribute most of it, about 80%, and fibrin the rest.
- **LY30 / ML** (lysis at 30 min / maximum lysis): breakdown of the clot. Elevated in hyperfibrinolysis. Treated with antifibrinolytics such as tranexamic acid.

**ROTEM channels** use different activators to isolate components:
- **EXTEM**: tissue factor (extrinsic pathway)
- **INTEM**: contact activation (intrinsic pathway)
- **FIBTEM**: adds cytochalasin D to block platelets, leaving fibrin-only strength
- **APTEM**: adds aprotinin or tranexamic acid. If lysis corrects, hyperfibrinolysis is confirmed.
- **HEPTEM**: adds heparinase to reveal heparin effect

Comparing channels is the point. Suppose EXTEM is weak and FIBTEM is weak: give fibrinogen. Suppose EXTEM is weak but FIBTEM is normal: the deficit is platelets.

**Uses.** VHAs are used in cardiac surgery, liver transplantation, major trauma and obstetric hemorrhage. Algorithms guide targeted, goal-directed replacement. This avoids empiric fixed-ratio transfusion.
levels.phd:
Viscoelastic assays translate polymer mechanics into hemostatic phenotype. The measured amplitude relates nonlinearly to the clot's shear elastic modulus G. One TEG-derived form is G = 5000·MA/(100−MA) dyn/cm². A small rise in MA at the high end therefore represents a large rise in clot stiffness. This nonlinearity matters when interpreting "hypercoagulable" high MA values.

**Component partitioning.** FIBTEM uses cytochalasin D, an actin polymerization inhibitor, to block platelet contraction. Some TEG functional-fibrinogen assays use a GPIIb/IIIa antagonist instead. Subtracting the fibrin contribution from total firmness gives an estimate of platelet-derived firmness. FIBTEM A5 or A10 (amplitude at 5 or 10 minutes) correlates with Clauss fibrinogen. It is also affected by hematocrit, because red cells dilute the fibrin network and lower measured firmness. Factor XIII deficiency weakens cross-linking and can reduce MCF despite normal fibrinogen.

**What they miss.** VHAs run without flow and without endothelium. They are largely insensitive to:
- von Willebrand factor function, which needs high shear
- aspirin and P2Y12 inhibitors, because thrombin overrides the ADP and thromboxane pathways
- low-molecular-weight heparin and direct oral anticoagulants, which have variable effects unless device-specific channels are used

**Platelet mapping.** TEG PlateletMapping uses reptilase plus factor XIIIa without thrombin, then adds ADP or arachidonic acid, to unmask antiplatelet effects.

**Fibrinolysis phenotypes.** Moore and colleagues described three phenotypes in trauma:
- **Hyperfibrinolysis** (high LY30)
- **Physiologic lysis**
- **Fibrinolysis shutdown** (very low LY30)

Both extremes were associated with higher mortality. This U-shaped curve argues against blanket antifibrinolysis. It sits awkwardly beside CRASH-2, which showed a mortality benefit from early tranexamic acid given to all bleeding trauma patients.

**Evidence.** Gonzalez et al. (2016) ran a single-center RCT in massive trauma transfusion. TEG-guided resuscitation improved survival over conventional coagulation-test guidance. The larger multicenter ITACTIC trial (Baksaas-Aasen et al., 2021) found no overall difference in the primary outcome between VHA-guided and conventional-test-guided protocols. A possible benefit appeared in severe traumatic brain injury. Cardiac surgery meta-analyses (Cochrane) show reduced transfusion and bleeding, with less certain effects on mortality.
levels.expert:
In practice, VHAs earn their value through algorithms, not curves. Most transfusion reductions come from replacing reflexive plasma with targeted fibrinogen and platelets, with prompt antifibrinolysis, and with recognizing when bleeding is surgical rather than coagulopathic. A normal trace in a patient who is still hemorrhaging should send the team back to the operative field.

**Pitfalls clinicians actually hit:**
- **Pre-analytic error**: sampling from heparinized lines, delayed analysis, wrong citrate fill ratio, or a cold sample. VHAs run at 37 °C by default and so mask hypothermic coagulopathy unless the patient's temperature is entered.
- **Hypercoagulable false comfort**: a normal trace does not exclude thrombotic risk. Prediction of venous thromboembolism from high MA is inconsistent.
- **Hidden drugs**: antiplatelet effect and direct oral anticoagulants can go unseen. Device-specific direct oral anticoagulant channels exist, such as RVV-based and ecarin-based assays, but drug levels are often better.
- **Device non-interchangeability**: TEG and ROTEM values are not numerically equivalent. Cartridge systems, such as TEG 6s, ClotPro and Quantra, need their own validated thresholds.
- **Time trap**: early amplitudes (A5, A10) predict MCF well, so waiting for full LY60 delays care.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Traumatic brain injury releases tissue factor and drives early hyperfibrinolysis that can turn to shutdown. Small hemostatic failures expand contusions. Subgroup signals from ITACTIC, and observational data, motivate VHA use in traumatic brain injury. However, tranexamic acid timing (CRASH-3), not VHA guidance, holds the stronger evidence base. In elective cranial surgery, the main use is identifying fibrinogen deficits during large-volume blood loss.

**Frontiers and open questions:**
- **Obstetrics**: in postpartum hemorrhage, FIBTEM A5 below about 12 mm predicts progression. The OBS2 trial suggested fibrinogen replacement helps only when FIBTEM is low, supporting threshold-guided therapy.
- **Liver disease**: VHAs reveal rebalanced hemostasis that the INR exaggerates, and they reduce prophylactic plasma before procedures.
- **Pediatrics and ECMO**: adoption is growing, but validated thresholds for children are scarce.
- **Next-generation devices**: platforms that incorporate flow, shear and endothelium aim to capture von Willebrand factor and platelet adhesion, which current static assays miss.
- **Unresolved**: whether fibrinolysis-phenotype-directed tranexamic acid should replace universal early tranexamic acid. Hard-outcome evidence is still lacking.

keyPoints: TEG and ROTEM measure the strength of a whole-blood clot over time
PT and aPTT stop at first fibrin; viscoelastic tests show the whole clot
R/CT reflects clotting factors, MA/MCF clot strength, LY30/ML breakdown
FIBTEM blocks platelets to show the fibrin contribution
Results guide targeted fibrinogen, platelets, plasma or tranexamic acid
Blind spots: aspirin, P2Y12 drugs, von Willebrand factor, hypothermia

test.q: What do TEG and ROTEM measure?
choices: Clot strength in whole blood over time
Time to first fibrin in separated plasma
The number of red cells per microliter
test.explain: Viscoelastic tests track the mechanical firmness of a forming whole-blood clot, unlike PT and aPTT, which time plasma clotting.

test.q: A prolonged R time (TEG) or CT (ROTEM) mainly suggests:
choices: Excess fibrinolysis breaking down the clot
A high fibrinogen level in the plasma
A low platelet count or platelet dysfunction
test.explain: R and CT measure time to initial fibrin, which depends on clotting factors and is prolonged by heparin.

test.q: Most of the maximum clot strength (MA/MCF) comes from:
test.explain: Platelets contribute about 80% of maximum amplitude, and fibrin contributes the rest.

test.q: What does the FIBTEM channel add to the sample?
test.explain: Cytochalasin D stops platelet contraction, so FIBTEM shows fibrin-only clot strength. Heparinase is used in HEPTEM, and aprotinin in APTEM.

test.q: EXTEM firmness is low but FIBTEM is normal. The most likely deficit is:
test.explain: Normal fibrin strength with weak total strength points to a platelet deficit.

test.q: A high LY30 on TEG indicates:
test.explain: LY30 is the percentage of clot lysis at 30 minutes. High values mean the clot breaks down too early.

test.q: Why are standard PT and aPTT limited in a bleeding patient?
choices: They stop at first fibrin and leave out platelets
They take several days to return a result
They measure the patient's red cell antibodies
They are run on whole blood at room temperature
test.explain: Plasma tests stop timing at the first fibrin strands and exclude platelets and red cells, so they miss clot strength and lysis.

test.q: Which ROTEM channel confirms hyperfibrinolysis when lysis corrects?
test.explain: APTEM adds an antifibrinolytic. If lysis seen in EXTEM corrects in APTEM, hyperfibrinolysis is confirmed.

test.q: Viscoelastic tests are poorly sensitive to which drug class?
test.explain: Thrombin in the assay overrides the ADP pathway, so standard traces miss P2Y12 inhibitors and aspirin. Platelet mapping is needed to detect them.

test.q: What is the full name of TEG?
test.explain: TEG stands for thromboelastography. ROTEM stands for rotational thromboelastometry.

test.q: The breakdown of a clot, measured by LY30 or ML, is called ___.
test.explain: Fibrinolysis is the breakdown of fibrin by plasmin. Excess can be treated with tranexamic acid.

test.q: Name the antifibrinolytic drug often given for hyperfibrinolysis.
test.explain: Tranexamic acid blocks plasminogen activation and was studied in CRASH-2 and CRASH-3.

kidTest.q: What do these machines watch blood do?
kidTest.explain: They watch a tiny drop of blood turn into a clot and feel how strong it gets.

kidTest.q: What is a clot like?
kidTest.explain: Like jelly, blood goes from runny to thick and wobbly.

kidTest.q: Why does a clot matter after a cut?
kidTest.explain: The clot forms a plug that stops bleeding.

kidTest.q: If the clot is weak, what can doctors do?
kidTest.explain: The machine shows what is missing, so doctors can give exactly that.

kidTest.q: Blood turns into a plug called a c _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: A clot is the plug that stops bleeding.

advancedTest.q: Using G = 5000·MA/(100−MA), why does a small rise in an already high MA matter?
choices: High MA mainly reflects a longer clotting time
Clot stiffness rises steeply as MA nears 100
MA saturates, so high values carry no meaning
Clot elasticity scales linearly with amplitude
advancedTest.explain: The denominator shrinks as MA approaches 100, so stiffness rises sharply. This makes high MA values hard to interpret.

advancedTest.q: Moore's U-shaped trauma data, linking both high and very low LY30 to mortality, best supports:
choices: Treating fibrinolysis shutdown with tranexamic acid
Giving antifibrinolytics to each trauma patient
Abandoning viscoelastic testing in major trauma
advancedTest.explain: If shutdown is also harmful, giving tranexamic acid to everyone may not suit every patient, which creates tension with CRASH-2.

advancedTest.q: A bleeding patient at 33 °C has a normal ROTEM. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: FIBTEM reflects core temperature, so it reads high
Cytochalasin D in EXTEM corrected the platelet deficit
Hypothermia shortens CT, which cancels out factor loss
The assay ran at 37 °C, masking hypothermic coagulopathy
advancedTest.explain: Viscoelastic tests warm samples to 37 °C by default. They miss cold-induced coagulopathy unless the patient's temperature is entered, and surgical bleeding should also be considered.

advancedTest.q: FIBTEM A5 underestimates fibrinogen in a patient with high hematocrit. The best reason is:
choices: Red cells release plasmin, which digests the fibrin
High hematocrit activates the cytochalasin D in the cup
Red cells raise factor XIII cross-linking in the clot
Red cells dilute the fibrin network and lower its firmness
advancedTest.explain: Red cells occupy volume within the clot and dilute the fibrin network, so measured firmness falls, separate from the true fibrinogen level.

lessons.title: Patient Blood Management & Hemostasis in Neurosurgery

levels.kid:
Blood is precious. Every bag in a hospital came from a kind person who gave it. So doctors try to use as little as they can. This plan is called **Patient Blood Management**.

It has three big ideas:
- Make the patient's own blood strong before surgery, like filling a car's tank before a long trip.
- Lose less blood during the operation.
- Help the body cope while it makes new blood afterward.

Brain surgeons have to be extra careful. The skull is like a closed box. Even a little bleeding inside it can squeeze the brain. So they use special tools that seal tiny blood vessels. They also use medicines that help clots hold together.
levels.hs:
**Patient Blood Management (PBM)** is a hospital-wide approach that puts the patient's own blood first. Instead of reaching for donated blood automatically, teams try to prevent the need for it. The World Health Organization calls it a patient-safety priority.

PBM rests on three "pillars":
- **Optimize the patient's red cell mass.** Find and treat **anemia** (too few red cells or too little hemoglobin) before planned surgery, often with iron.
- **Minimize blood loss.** Use careful surgical technique and tools that seal vessels. Drugs like **tranexamic acid** slow the breakdown of clots. Cell salvage collects shed blood and returns it to the patient.
- **Harness tolerance of anemia.** Give a transfusion based on need, not habit. Many stable patients do well with a lower hemoglobin.

Why does this matter? Transfusions can cause reactions, fluid overload and immune effects, and blood supplies are limited. Studies of PBM programs show fewer transfusions with outcomes that are as good or better.

Neurosurgery adds special risks. The skull cannot expand, so bleeding raises **intracranial pressure**. For example, a patient on the blood thinner warfarin who has a brain bleed needs that drug reversed quickly. Surgeons use **bipolar cautery** and topical agents such as gelatin or oxidized cellulose to stop oozing.
levels.college:
PBM is an evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategy built around three pillars, each applied before, during and after surgery.

**Pillar 1: Optimize erythropoiesis.** Preoperative anemia is common and independently predicts transfusion and complications. Work-up starts with ferritin and transferrin saturation. Iron deficiency is treated with oral or intravenous iron, and erythropoiesis-stimulating agents are used in selected cases. Elective surgery is ideally delayed until anemia is corrected.

**Pillar 2: Minimize blood loss.**
- **Antifibrinolytics:** tranexamic acid (TXA) is a lysine analogue. It blocks the lysine-binding sites on plasminogen, so plasminogen cannot bind fibrin and fibrinolysis slows.
- **Cell salvage:** shed blood is suctioned, washed and reinfused. It is used with caution in tumor surgery because of theoretical seeding of tumor cells.
- **Point-of-care testing** targets specific defects (covered in the viscoelastic lesson).
- **Reduce iatrogenic loss:** smaller blood-draw tubes and fewer routine labs.

**Pillar 3: Tolerate anemia.** Restrictive thresholds (transfuse below about 7 g/dL hemoglobin in most stable adults) were supported by TRICC and later trials.

**Neurosurgical specifics:**
- **Anticoagulant reversal:** for warfarin, four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC) plus vitamin K; idarucizumab for dabigatran; andexanet alfa or PCC for factor Xa inhibitors.
- **Antiplatelet agents:** platelet transfusion for antiplatelet-associated spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) without surgery *worsened* outcomes in the PATCH trial.
- **Local hemostasis:** bipolar coagulation, gelatin sponge, oxidized cellulose, thrombin-based sealants, bone wax.
- **Blood pressure** control limits hematoma expansion.

The brain is unforgiving: a few milliliters of rebleeding in the posterior fossa can be fatal, so hemostasis there is more critical than raw blood volume.
levels.phd:
PBM reframes transfusion as a decision with its own risk. Observational data link red cell transfusion to infection, thrombosis and transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO). Biologically plausible mechanisms include the **storage lesion** (2,3-DPG depletion, nitric-oxide scavenging by free hemoglobin, microvesicles) and immunomodulation. Confounding by indication is severe, however, so randomized threshold trials are the real evidence base.

The brain injury setting challenges the restrictive paradigm. Cerebral oxygen delivery depends on hemoglobin, and anemia triggers compensatory cerebral vasodilation that may exhaust reserve in injured tissue. Key trials:
- **TRICC** (1999) and **TRISS** supported thresholds near 7 g/dL in critical care.
- **Robertson et al. (JAMA 2014)**: in traumatic brain injury (TBI), a 10 g/dL threshold did not improve 6-month outcome and raised thromboembolic events.
- **HEMOTION (2024)** in TBI and **TRAIN (2024)** in acute brain injury (subarachnoid hemorrhage, ICH, TBI) leaned toward benefit from liberal transfusion, so neuro-specific thresholds remain unsettled.

TXA pharmacology: at low concentrations it competitively inhibits plasminogen lysine-binding kringle domains. At high concentrations it can antagonize GABA-A and glycine receptors, which explains seizure risk, a real concern in neurosurgery. Clinical trials:
- **CRASH-3** (2019, about 12,700 TBI patients): TXA within 3 hours reduced head-injury death in mild-to-moderate TBI, with no benefit in severe TBI.
- **TICH-2**: in spontaneous ICH, TXA reduced hematoma expansion and early death but did not change 90-day function.
- **ULTRA**: in aneurysmal SAH, TXA did not significantly reduce rebleeding or improve outcome.

The recurring pattern is that biologic hemostatic effects do not reliably become functional benefit.

On reversal agents, **ANNEXA-I** (2024) showed andexanet improved hemostatic efficacy over usual care (mostly PCC) in factor Xa inhibitor-associated ICH, at the cost of more thrombotic events, including ischemic stroke. Recombinant factor VIIa in ICH (FAST trial) reduced hematoma growth without functional gain. The FASTEST trial is re-testing it with ultra-early delivery.
levels.expert:
Practical PBM in neurosurgery starts in clinic. Screen for anemia at least 3-4 weeks before elective cranial or complex spine surgery so that intravenous iron has time to work. Plan perioperative anticoagulation using drug half-life and renal function, and coordinate antiplatelet holds with cardiology. Stopping dual antiplatelet therapy early after a coronary stent risks stent thrombosis, so for urgent cases surgery may proceed on aspirin.

Pitfalls:
- **Point-of-care testing has blind spots.** Standard viscoelastic assays and conventional coagulation tests are relatively insensitive to aspirin and P2Y12 inhibitors and to direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs). Platelet function assays and drug-specific levels (anti-Xa calibrated, dilute thrombin time) fill the gap but are often unavailable at night.
- **TXA is not free.** Seizure risk and possible delayed cerebral ischemia after SAH temper enthusiasm. In the GI bleeding trial HALT-IT, TXA increased venous thromboembolism.
- **Andexanet interferes with heparin.** It is linked to heparin resistance during later cardiopulmonary bypass or neurovascular procedures.
- **Fluid strategy matters.** Hypotonic fluids worsen cerebral edema, and large volumes dilute clotting factors. Synthetic colloids (hydroxyethyl starch) impair fibrin polymerization and are largely abandoned.
- **Hypothermia, acidosis and hypocalcemia** silently degrade coagulation during long cases. Ionized calcium deserves monitoring.

Spine surgery is the strongest neurosurgical PBM use case. Multilevel fusions and deformity correction bleed heavily, and TXA and cell salvage have meta-analytic support for reducing transfusion. Cell salvage in metastatic spine tumor surgery is increasingly accepted with leukocyte-depletion filters, though guidance is still evolving.

Also relevant:
- **Jehovah's Witness patients**, who decline transfusion, show that bloodless neurosurgery is feasible with meticulous PBM.
- **Organizational levers** such as electronic decision support, single-unit transfusion policies ("why give two when one will do") and audit feedback drive much of the measured benefit.

Open questions: individualized neuro transfusion triggers guided by brain tissue oxygen (PbtO2) or near-infrared spectroscopy; the best reversal agent for factor Xa inhibitor-associated ICH given ANNEXA-I's thrombosis signal; whether ultra-early hemostatic therapy can finally convert reduced hematoma growth into functional recovery; and the safety of desmopressin for antiplatelet-associated ICH, which still lacks definitive trials.

keyPoints: Patient Blood Management puts the patient's own blood first, before donor transfusion
Three pillars: optimize red cell mass, minimize blood loss, tolerate anemia
Tranexamic acid blocks plasminogen's lysine-binding sites to slow fibrinolysis
Restrictive thresholds (about 7 g/dL) suit most adults; brain injury thresholds are debated
Reverse anticoagulants fast in brain bleeds: PCC, idarucizumab, andexanet
The closed skull makes small rebleeds dangerous, so local hemostasis is critical

test.q: Which is one of the three pillars of Patient Blood Management?
choices: Transfuse two units for each surgery
Optimize the patient's red cell mass
test.explain: The pillars are optimizing red cell mass, minimizing blood loss and tolerating anemia. Routine two-unit transfusion goes against PBM.

test.q: How does tranexamic acid reduce bleeding?
choices: It blocks plasminogen binding to fibrin
test.explain: TXA is a lysine analogue that occupies plasminogen's lysine-binding sites, which slows fibrinolysis. It does not supply clotting factors.

test.q: Why is bleeding especially dangerous in brain surgery?
choices: Cautery is unsafe to use near the brain
Brain tissue is unable to form clots
The rigid skull lets pressure build up
Brain blood is lacking in platelets
test.explain: The rigid skull means even small hematomas raise intracranial pressure.

test.q: A restrictive transfusion threshold for most stable adults is about:
test.explain: TRICC and later trials supported transfusing below about 7 g/dL in most stable adults.

test.q: Which drug is used to reverse dabigatran?
test.explain: Idarucizumab is an antibody fragment that binds dabigatran. Andexanet targets factor Xa inhibitors.

test.q: What did the PATCH trial find about platelet transfusion in antiplatelet-associated ICH?
test.explain: In PATCH, platelet transfusion for antiplatelet-associated ICH without surgery led to worse outcomes.

test.q: Cell salvage is used with caution in tumor surgery because of:
test.explain: Reinfused shed blood could in theory carry tumor cells, though leukocyte-depletion filters are increasingly used.

test.q: Before planned surgery, iron deficiency anemia is best handled by:
choices: Ignoring it if the patient is young
test.explain: Pillar 1: find and treat anemia before surgery, often with oral or intravenous iron.

test.q: Which is a topical hemostatic agent used in neurosurgery?
test.explain: Oxidized cellulose, gelatin sponge, thrombin sealants and bone wax help stop local oozing.

test.q: For warfarin-associated brain bleeding, teams give four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate plus vitamin ___.
test.explain: PCC replaces clotting factors fast, and vitamin K restores the body's own production of them.

test.q: What is the abbreviation for the hospital approach that prioritizes a patient's own blood over donor transfusion?
test.explain: PBM stands for Patient Blood Management.

test.q: Too few red cells or too little hemoglobin is called ___.
test.explain: Anemia raises transfusion risk, so PBM treats it before surgery.

kidTest.q: Why do doctors try to use less donated blood?
choices: Blood is too heavy to carry
Donated blood is the wrong color
kidTest.explain: Every bag comes from a donor, so it should be used carefully.

kidTest.q: What is the skull like in the lesson?
kidTest.explain: The skull is like a closed box, so bleeding inside can squeeze the brain.

kidTest.q: What happens before surgery in the lesson's plan?
kidTest.explain: Like filling a car's tank, doctors make the patient's own blood strong first.

kidTest.q: What do special tools in brain surgery do?
kidTest.explain: They seal small vessels so less blood is lost.

kidTest.q: The blood bags in a hospital come from kind people called d _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Donors give their blood to help others.

advancedTest.q: CRASH-3, TICH-2 and ULTRA share which pattern?
choices: TXA increased rebleeding but improved long-term function
TXA showed no biological effect on bleeding in any trial
TXA worked mainly when given over 6 hours after injury
TXA had hemostatic effects that did not reliably improve function
advancedTest.explain: TXA reduced bleeding outcomes such as hematoma growth or rebleeding, but functional benefit was absent or limited.

advancedTest.q: Why might a strict restrictive threshold be less certain in acute brain injury than in general ICU care?
choices: Injured brain may lack reserve for low oxygen delivery
Restrictive thresholds raise intracranial pressure directly
Brain-injured patients react badly to stored red cells
Hemoglobin does not affect cerebral oxygen delivery
advancedTest.explain: Anemia triggers compensatory cerebral vasodilation that injured tissue may exhaust. TRAIN and HEMOTION leaned toward liberal transfusion.

advancedTest.q: A patient on apixaban needs urgent cranial surgery, and the viscoelastic test looks normal. The best interpretation is:
choices: Standard assays may miss DOAC effect; check a calibrated anti-Xa level
Apixaban effect is absent, so surgery is safe
The test proves that the drug was cleared by the kidneys
Platelet transfusion is indicated to restore hemostasis
advancedTest.explain: Standard viscoelastic and coagulation tests are relatively insensitive to DOACs, so drug-specific levels are needed.

advancedTest.q: ANNEXA-I creates a clinical trade-off because andexanet:
choices: Reversed dabigatran but not factor Xa inhibitors
Improved function but caused seizures from GABA-A blockade
Reduced thrombosis but worsened hematoma growth
Improved hemostasis but raised thrombotic events
advancedTest.explain: Andexanet improved hemostatic efficacy over usual care but increased thrombotic events, including ischemic stroke.

lessons.title: Gene Therapy & Gene Editing for Hemophilia and Sickle Cell

levels.kid:
Imagine every cell has a tiny instruction book called DNA. Some kids are born missing a page, like the instructions for making a blood 'glue' that stops bleeding. That's hemophilia. Other kids have a smudged page that makes blood cells shaped like crescent moons instead of round donuts, which hurts. That's sickle cell disease.

Scientists found ways to fix the book itself. They can use a tiny, harmless virus like a delivery truck to drop off a brand-new, correct instruction page. Or they can use molecular scissors called **CRISPR** to snip the DNA and wake up an old backup instruction that had fallen asleep.

These new treatments can be given once and work for years, instead of needing shots over and over.
levels.hs:
**Hemophilia A and B** are inherited conditions where the blood is missing a working copy of the gene for clotting factor VIII or IX. **Sickle cell disease** comes from a change in the beta-globin gene that makes red blood cells bend into a crescent shape and block small blood vessels.

For hemophilia, doctors now use **gene therapy**: a modified, harmless virus called **AAV** (adeno-associated virus) carries a correct copy of the factor gene into liver cells, which then make the missing clotting factor. Two approved examples are Hemgenix for hemophilia B and Roctavian for hemophilia A, each given as a single infusion meant to last for years.

For sickle cell disease, scientists use **gene editing** with CRISPR-Cas9, molecular scissors that cut DNA at an exact spot. The therapy Casgevy edits a gene called BCL11A, which normally shuts off fetal hemoglobin after birth. Turning it down brings back fetal hemoglobin, which stops sickling.

Both approaches aim to treat the disease at its root, in one treatment, rather than with lifelong injections or transfusions, though the process is intense and still new.
levels.college:
Hemophilia A and B arise from loss-of-function mutations in the X-linked F8 or F9 genes encoding clotting factors VIII and IX. Sickle cell disease comes from a single missense mutation in the beta-globin gene (HBB), producing hemoglobin S that polymerizes under low oxygen, deforming red cells into a sickle shape.

Two broad strategies now target the DNA itself:

- **In vivo gene therapy (AAV vectors).** AAV carrying a functional F8 or F9 transgene is infused intravenously and preferentially transduces hepatocytes, which then secrete the missing clotting factor. The AAV genome stays largely episomal (non-integrating), reducing insertional risk. Hemgenix delivers a hyperactive 'Padua' variant of factor IX for hemophilia B; Roctavian delivers factor VIII for hemophilia A. Both are single infusions intended to give years of elevated factor activity.

- **Ex vivo gene editing (CRISPR-Cas9).** For sickle cell disease, a patient's own hematopoietic stem cells are collected, edited outside the body, and reinfused after the native marrow is cleared with chemotherapy (myeloablative conditioning). Casgevy uses CRISPR-Cas9 to disrupt a regulatory enhancer of the BCL11A gene. BCL11A normally silences fetal hemoglobin production after birth, so disrupting its enhancer reactivates fetal hemoglobin, which dilutes hemoglobin S and blocks polymerization.

- **Lentiviral gene addition.** Lyfgenia instead inserts an anti-sickling beta-globin gene into stem cells using an integrating lentiviral vector.

Both ex vivo approaches share the same stem-cell harvest, conditioning, and engraftment process, and both aim at a durable, one-time functional correction rather than lifelong protein replacement or transfusion.
levels.phd:
AAV-based hemophilia gene therapy exploits the virus's hepatotropism and its capacity to persist as circular episomes within post-mitotic hepatocyte nuclei, largely avoiding chromosomal integration. Both approved products use AAV5 capsids with liver-specific promoters driving codon-optimized transgenes; Hemgenix additionally encodes the Padua R338L hyperactive factor IX variant, boosting specific activity several-fold. A major constraint is pre-existing anti-AAV neutralizing antibodies from prior natural infection, which exclude seropositive patients and preclude redosing. Transaminitis from a CD8+ T-cell response against transduced hepatocytes is common and managed with tapering corticosteroids, and can blunt transgene expression. Long-term follow-up (e.g., the HOPE-B trial) shows factor IX activity sustained in the mild-to-moderate range for several years, though some patients show gradual decline, plausibly from episome dilution during hepatocyte turnover or progressive immune clearance.

For sickle cell disease, exa-cel's design rests on human genetics: genome-wide association studies identified BCL11A as the dominant repressor of fetal hemoglobin, and finer mapping located an erythroid-lineage-restricted, GATA1-occupied enhancer (the +58 DNase I hypersensitivity site) whose disruption lowers BCL11A selectively in red cell precursors, sparing its roles in B-lymphopoiesis and neurodevelopment. CRISPR-Cas9 editing achieves allelic disruption in a large majority of alleles in the manufactured cell product, and clinical data show near-complete elimination of vaso-occlusive crises alongside pancellular fetal hemoglobin distribution exceeding 40% of total hemoglobin.

Lovo-cel's integrating lentiviral approach inserts an anti-sickling beta-globin variant semi-randomly across the genome. This recalls the cautionary history of X-linked SCID gene therapy, where gammaretroviral vectors activated the LMO2 proto-oncogene near integration sites, causing T-cell leukemias in several patients. Self-inactivating lentiviral vectors were designed to reduce such risk, yet reported hematologic malignancies in lovo-cel recipients have reopened debate about vector genotoxicity versus conditioning-related mutagenesis.
levels.expert:
Clinical deployment has outpaced some of the infrastructure needed to support these therapies. List prices for Hemgenix, Roctavian, Casgevy and Lyfgenia run into the millions of dollars per patient, prompting payers to experiment with outcomes-based annuity contracts that spread payment over years and claw back funds if factor levels or clinical response fail to persist. Regulators have mandated long-term follow-up studies spanning well over a decade to capture late toxicities and durability.

Lyfgenia now carries a boxed warning after several recipients developed myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukemia; investigation points toward vector integration near growth-regulating genes alongside possible contributions from busulfan-based conditioning, which is independently genotoxic. This has sharpened interest in non-integrating alternatives and in reducing conditioning intensity, an active area using targeted antibody-based conditioning to spare fertility and limit marrow toxicity.

The field is also moving from ex vivo toward in vivo editing. Early-phase programs are testing lipid-nanoparticle-delivered base editors aimed directly at the BCL11A enhancer in circulating stem cells, bypassing stem-cell harvest and myeloablation, and liver-directed in vivo gene-insertion strategies pair AAV-delivered CRISPR components with a corrective template to achieve precise, site-specific factor gene knock-in rather than episomal expression, potentially solving the durability problem seen with simple AAV delivery.

A pressing equity concern: sickle cell disease carries its highest burden in sub-Saharan Africa and other under-resourced health systems, where the cell-collection, conditioning, and sterile manufacturing infrastructure these therapies require is largely unavailable, so most treated patients so far are in high-income countries. Off-target editing surveillance, using unbiased genome-wide assays rather than predicted-site screening alone, remains an unresolved regulatory expectation as base and prime editors with distinct off-target profiles enter trials.

keyPoints: Hemophilia A/B result from missing factor VIII/IX; AAV vectors deliver a working gene copy mainly to liver cells
Hemgenix and Roctavian are approved AAV gene therapies giving sustained clotting factor expression from a single infusion
Sickle cell disease stems from a beta-globin mutation causing HbS polymerization and red cell sickling
Casgevy (exa-cel) uses CRISPR-Cas9 to disrupt the BCL11A erythroid enhancer, reactivating fetal hemoglobin to block sickling
Lyfgenia (lovo-cel) uses an integrating lentiviral vector and carries a boxed warning for blood cancer risk
Ex vivo cell therapies require stem cell collection, myeloablative conditioning, and long-term monitoring, at very high cost

test.q: What clotting factor is deficient in hemophilia B?
test.explain: Hemophilia B results from deficient or dysfunctional factor IX; factor VIII deficiency instead causes hemophilia A.

test.q: AAV gene therapy vectors for hemophilia are designed to mainly transduce which cell type?
test.explain: AAV5-based vectors are liver-tropic; transduced hepatocytes then secrete the clotting factor into the bloodstream.

test.q: Casgevy (exa-cel) treats sickle cell disease by disrupting which regulatory element?
test.explain: Exa-cel disrupts the erythroid-specific enhancer of BCL11A, de-repressing fetal hemoglobin production.

test.q: Why does reactivating fetal hemoglobin reduce sickling?
choices: It dilutes hemoglobin S, blocking polymerization
It raises oxygen delivery directly to tissues
It directly removes hemoglobin S from red blood cells
It increases red blood cell membrane rigidity
test.explain: Fetal hemoglobin interferes with HbS polymer formation, reducing sickling even though HbS is still present.

test.q: Lyfgenia (lovo-cel) uses which vector to deliver an anti-sickling beta-globin gene?
test.explain: Lovo-cel uses an integrating lentiviral vector, unlike the episomal AAV vectors used in hemophilia gene therapy.

test.q: Why do integrating lentiviral vectors carry a risk of blood cancer?
choices: They degrade the recipient's own DNA repair genes
They can insert near genes that control cell growth
test.explain: Integration near growth-regulating genes can activate oncogenes, a mechanism called insertional mutagenesis.

test.q: What pretreatment prepares the marrow before infusing edited stem cells?
test.explain: Conditioning, such as busulfan, clears existing marrow so that edited stem cells can engraft.

test.q: Why might pre-existing antibodies block AAV gene therapy from working?
choices: They destroy the clotting factor protein once produced
They prevent conditioning chemotherapy from working
They neutralize the viral vector before it can enter cells
test.explain: Neutralizing antibodies from prior natural AAV exposure can prevent the vector from transducing cells, excluding some patients.

test.q: How does AAV-based gene therapy generally differ from CRISPR-based gene editing in these diseases?
choices: AAV edits the genome permanently, while CRISPR stays episomal
AAV mainly adds episomal DNA copies, while CRISPR directly edits the genome
AAV works mainly in red blood cells, while CRISPR works in the liver
AAV requires stem cell collection, while CRISPR does not
test.explain: AAV vectors largely remain non-integrated episomes delivering extra gene copies, whereas CRISPR-Cas9 makes targeted permanent edits to genomic DNA.

test.q: What is the brand name of the FDA-approved CRISPR gene-editing therapy for sickle cell disease?
test.explain: Casgevy (exa-cel) is the CRISPR-Cas9 cell therapy approved for sickle cell disease.

test.q: Hemgenix delivers a gene encoding a hyperactive version of clotting factor ___.
test.explain: Hemgenix encodes the Padua variant of factor IX for treating hemophilia B.

test.q: What gene is targeted in sickle cell gene editing to raise fetal hemoglobin levels?
test.explain: Disrupting BCL11A's erythroid enhancer de-represses fetal hemoglobin production.

kidTest.q: What problem does hemophilia cause in the body?
kidTest.explain: Hemophilia means the blood is missing a clotting factor, so it's slow to form a clot.

kidTest.q: What shape do red blood cells take in sickle cell disease?
kidTest.explain: The changed hemoglobin makes red cells bend into a crescent, or sickle, shape.

kidTest.q: What do scientists use to deliver a new gene into cells?
kidTest.explain: A modified, harmless virus called AAV can carry a correct gene copy into cells.

kidTest.q: What tool do scientists use like scissors to cut DNA?
kidTest.explain: CRISPR acts like molecular scissors that cut DNA at an exact spot.

kidTest.q: What is the name of the DNA-cutting tool? (c _ _ _ _ _)
kidTest.explain: CRISPR-Cas9 is the gene-editing tool used to fix DNA at a precise location.

advancedTest.q: AAV-delivered factor IX activity sometimes declines gradually over years after treatment, even though AAV genomes mostly stay episomal. What best explains this?
choices: The AAV capsid mutates and loses infectivity inside the body
Hepatocyte turnover dilutes episomes, with immune clearance
Host enzymes actively excise the transgene within days
The transgene promoter is degraded by stomach acid
advancedTest.explain: Episomal DNA does not replicate with cell division, so hepatocyte turnover combined with possible immune clearance of transduced cells can reduce long-term expression.

advancedTest.q: Why does disrupting the BCL11A erythroid enhancer avoid impairing BCL11A's role in B-lymphocyte development?
choices: BCL11A has no separate role in B-lymphocyte development
The enhancer is active specifically in erythroid cells, not in B lymphocytes
The edited stem cells are transplanted into the spleen instead of bone marrow
CRISPR editing targets a different gene in lymphocyte precursors
advancedTest.explain: The +58 enhancer region is erythroid-lineage-specific, so disrupting it lowers BCL11A selectively in red cell precursors while other regulatory elements keep it active in lymphocytes.

advancedTest.q: The historic X-linked SCID gene therapy trials that caused T-cell leukemia primarily implicated which mechanism?
choices: CRISPR off-target cutting in tumor suppressor genes
Myeloablative conditioning alone causing DNA damage
Gammaretroviral vector integration activating the LMO2 oncogene
advancedTest.explain: Gammaretroviral vectors used in early SCID-X1 trials integrated near LMO2, activating this proto-oncogene and causing leukemia in several patients.

advancedTest.q: Why is myeloablative conditioning typically required before infusing CRISPR-edited stem cells for sickle cell disease?
choices: To raise antibody levels against sickle hemoglobin
To reduce the total number of red cells needed for transfusion
To permanently inactivate the CRISPR enzyme before infusion
To clear marrow space so edited stem cells can engraft
advancedTest.explain: Conditioning clears existing marrow, giving infused edited stem cells room to engraft and gradually replace the patient's diseased hematopoietic stem cells.

lessons.title: Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation & Graft-versus-Host Disease

levels.kid:
Deep inside your bones is soft stuff called **marrow**. It is like a factory that makes all your blood cells, every single day.

Sometimes the factory breaks, or it starts making bad cells, like in some cancers. Then doctors can give the person a brand-new factory! They take special "seed" cells, called **stem cells**, from a healthy helper called a **donor**. The seeds travel through the blood and settle in the bones. Then they grow a new factory.

But there is a tricky part. The new cells bring their own tiny guards. Sometimes those guards think the patient's body is a stranger and attack it. Doctors call this **graft-versus-host disease**. They use medicines to calm the guards down.
levels.hs:
**Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs)** live in the bone marrow and can make every type of blood cell: red cells, white cells and platelets. A **hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT)** replaces a patient's blood-forming system.

There are two main types:
- **Autologous**: the patient's own stem cells are collected, stored, and given back after very strong chemotherapy. This is common in **multiple myeloma** and lymphoma.
- **Allogeneic**: the cells come from another person, the **donor**. This is used for leukemias, marrow failure such as severe **aplastic anemia**, and some inherited diseases like **sickle cell disease**.

Before transplant, the patient gets **conditioning**: chemotherapy, sometimes with radiation, to destroy the old marrow and weaken the immune system so the graft is not rejected. Stem cells can come from bone marrow, from blood (after drugs push them out of the marrow), or from umbilical cord blood.

Donors are matched by **HLA** proteins, which are "ID tags" on cells. A sibling is the classic best match.

The big danger in allogeneic transplant is **graft-versus-host disease (GVHD)**. Donor T cells attack the patient's skin, gut and liver. There is a helpful twin effect, though: those same donor T cells can attack leftover cancer cells. This is called the **graft-versus-leukemia** effect.
levels.college:
HSCT rescues or replaces hematopoiesis. HSCs are identified clinically by the surface marker **CD34**, and graft dose is counted in CD34+ cells.

**Sources**
- **Bone marrow** harvest from the iliac crest.
- **Peripheral blood stem cells (PBSC)**, mobilized with G-CSF (filgrastim) with or without **plerixafor**, a CXCR4 antagonist that releases HSCs from marrow niches. PBSC grafts engraft faster but carry more chronic GVHD.
- **Umbilical cord blood**, which tolerates more HLA mismatch but has a low cell dose and slow engraftment.

**Conditioning**
- **Myeloablative** regimens, such as busulfan/cyclophosphamide or total body irradiation, give maximal tumor kill and high toxicity.
- **Reduced-intensity** regimens rely mainly on graft-versus-tumor immunity. They let older or frailer patients undergo transplant.

**HLA matching.** HLA-A, -B, -C and -DRB1 are typed at high resolution (an "8/8 match"). Each sibling has a 25% chance of being a full match. Other options include matched unrelated donors from registries, cord blood, and **haploidentical** (half-matched) family donors.

**Engraftment** is usually defined as an absolute neutrophil count above 0.5 x 10^9/L on 3 consecutive days. It typically comes 2-3 weeks after PBSC grafts. Before engraftment, infection and mucositis dominate.

**GVHD** requires three things (Billingham's criteria):
- immunocompetent graft cells
- a host that cannot reject them
- antigenic disparity between donor and host

**Acute GVHD** targets the skin (maculopapular rash, often on the palms and soles), the gut (large-volume diarrhea) and the liver (cholestasis with raised bilirubin). It is graded I-IV.

**Chronic GVHD** resembles autoimmune disease: sclerotic skin, dry eyes and mouth, and **bronchiolitis obliterans** in the lungs.

Prophylaxis classically combines a calcineurin inhibitor (tacrolimus or cyclosporine) with methotrexate. First-line treatment is corticosteroids.
levels.phd:
Acute GVHD pathogenesis is classically modeled in three phases (Ferrara).

- **Phase 1:** conditioning damages tissues, especially the intestinal epithelium. This releases DAMPs and PAMPs and drives a TNF, IL-1 and IL-6 "cytokine storm" that activates host antigen-presenting cells.
- **Phase 2:** donor T cells recognize either mismatched HLA or **minor histocompatibility antigens**, which are polymorphic peptides presented by matched HLA. That is why GVHD still occurs in HLA-identical sibling transplants. Activated T cells proliferate and polarize toward Th1/Th17, signaling through **JAK1/2**.
- **Phase 3:** effector cells and cytokines cause apoptosis of target epithelia. Damage to intestinal crypts, including loss of Paneth cells and of Lgr5+ stem cells, amplifies the cycle.

The gut microbiome modulates risk. Loss of diversity and of butyrate-producing Clostridia correlates with worse GVHD and survival, as shown in Memorial Sloan Kettering cohorts.

Chronic GVHD is mechanistically distinct. It involves thymic damage with impaired negative selection, aberrant B-cell activation (with BAFF excess and alloantibodies), defective regulatory T cells, and macrophage-driven TGF-beta fibrosis.

These mechanisms have produced approved targeted drugs:
- **ruxolitinib** (a JAK1/2 inhibitor; REACH2 and REACH3 trials) for steroid-refractory acute and chronic GVHD
- **ibrutinib** and **belumosudil** (a ROCK2 inhibitor) for chronic GVHD
- **axatilimab**, a CSF-1R antibody that depletes pathogenic macrophages

The **graft-versus-leukemia (GVL)** effect was proven by several lines of evidence:
- higher relapse after syngeneic (identical twin) or T-cell-depleted grafts
- lower relapse in patients who develop GVHD
- remissions induced by **donor lymphocyte infusion** in relapsed CML (Kolb, 1990)

The central tension is separating GVL from GVHD. **Post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy)**, developed by the Johns Hopkins group, selectively kills alloreactive T cells that are proliferating early after transplant. Regulatory T cells survive because they express high levels of aldehyde dehydrogenase. PTCy made haploidentical transplantation practical. The BMT CTN 1703 trial showed that PTCy/tacrolimus/MMF beat tacrolimus/methotrexate on GVHD-free, relapse-free survival (GRFS) in reduced-intensity matched transplants.
levels.expert:
Practical decisions now revolve around composite endpoints such as **GRFS**. Simply surviving with severe chronic GVHD is no longer counted as success.

**Donor choice and access.** Matched unrelated donor probability varies sharply by ancestry. It is lower for patients of African, Asian or mixed descent because of HLA diversity. PTCy-based haploidentical and mismatched unrelated donor transplants (ACCESS trial) have largely closed this gap. Cord blood use has declined accordingly. Donor-specific anti-HLA antibodies in the recipient predict **graft failure** and should be screened for before mismatched transplants.

**Risk stratification.** The **MAGIC algorithm probability** combines serum ST2 and REG3-alpha early after transplant or at GVHD onset. It predicts non-relapse mortality and steroid resistance better than clinical grade alone. It is being used to trial treatment tailored to risk. Clinical grading via the MAGIC criteria for acute GVHD and the NIH 2014 consensus for chronic GVHD is essential for comparing studies.

**Diagnostic pitfalls.**
- Skin rash may be a drug eruption or engraftment syndrome.
- Diarrhea may be *C. difficile*, CMV colitis or mycophenolate toxicity. Biopsy showing crypt apoptosis supports GVHD but is not specific.
- Liver dysfunction may be **sinusoidal obstruction syndrome** (painful hepatomegaly, weight gain, high bilirubin), treated with defibrotide, or drug injury.

**Infection.** **Letermovir** prophylaxis has reduced clinically significant CMV infection. EBV-driven post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder is a risk after T-cell depletion and ATG. Prolonged immune reconstitution means patients need full revaccination.

**Neurological complications** are relevant to a neurosurgical career:
- calcineurin-inhibitor-associated **posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome**
- HHV-6 limbic encephalitis, especially after cord grafts
- intracranial hemorrhage during thrombocytopenia
- invasive fungal brain abscesses, which may need neurosurgical biopsy

**Open questions** include several areas:
- microbiome restoration, including fecal microbiota transplantation, for steroid-refractory gut GVHD
- regulatory T-cell-enriched engineered grafts (e.g., Orca-T)
- cheaper, less toxic conditioning using antibody-drug conjugates against CD117 or CD45, which matters for nonmalignant disease
- how allogeneic transplant's role shifts as CAR-T cells and bispecific antibodies advance

keyPoints: HSCT replaces blood-forming marrow using CD34+ stem cells
Autologous uses the patient's own cells; allogeneic uses a donor
Conditioning destroys old marrow and suppresses immunity
HLA matching is key; haploidentical transplant works with PTCy
GVHD: donor T cells attack skin, gut, liver (and more in chronic)
Graft-versus-leukemia is the beneficial flip side of GVHD

test.q: In an autologous transplant, the stem cells come from:
test.explain: Autologous means self. The patient's own cells are collected and returned after high-dose chemotherapy.

test.q: Which three organs are the classic targets of acute GVHD?
test.explain: Acute GVHD typically causes rash, diarrhea and cholestatic liver injury.

test.q: What is the main purpose of conditioning before an allogeneic transplant?
choices: To clear marrow and blunt host immunity
To boost the patient's red cell count
To test the donor's HLA type
To harvest stem cells from the blood
test.explain: Conditioning ablates the diseased marrow and suppresses the host immune system so the graft is not rejected.

test.q: Plerixafor helps stem cell mobilization by blocking:
test.explain: Plerixafor antagonizes CXCR4, releasing HSCs from their marrow niches into the blood.

test.q: What is the chance that any one full sibling is a full HLA match?
test.explain: Each child inherits one of two HLA haplotypes from each parent, giving a 1 in 4 chance of a full match.

test.q: The graft-versus-leukemia effect refers to:
choices: Donor T cells attacking cancer cells
Host cells rejecting the donor graft
test.explain: Donor immune cells recognize and kill residual malignant cells. This is the beneficial side of alloreactivity.

test.q: Bronchiolitis obliterans and sclerotic skin are features of:
test.explain: Chronic GVHD resembles autoimmune or fibrotic disease, affecting the skin, glands and lungs.

test.q: Compared with bone marrow grafts, peripheral blood stem cell grafts tend to:
test.explain: PBSC grafts contain more cells and T cells, which speeds engraftment but increases chronic GVHD.

test.q: Classic GVHD prophylaxis combines methotrexate with a:
test.explain: Tacrolimus or cyclosporine, which are calcineurin inhibitors, plus methotrexate is the traditional prophylaxis.

test.q: Which cell surface marker is used to count hematopoietic stem cells in a graft?
test.explain: Graft dose is measured in CD34+ cells per kilogram.

test.q: Donors are matched by ___ proteins, the cell 'ID tags'.
test.explain: Human leukocyte antigens determine immune compatibility between donor and host.

test.q: A half-matched family donor transplant is called ___.
test.explain: Haploidentical donors share one HLA haplotype with the patient.

kidTest.q: Where does your body make blood cells?
kidTest.explain: Marrow inside bones is the blood-cell factory.

kidTest.q: What is a donor?
choices: A healthy helper who gives cells
kidTest.explain: A donor gives their healthy stem cells to the patient.

kidTest.q: What do stem cells do after they arrive?
kidTest.explain: They settle in the bones and make new blood cells.

kidTest.q: In graft-versus-host disease, what goes wrong?
kidTest.explain: The donor's immune guards mistake the patient's body for a stranger.

kidTest.q: The special seed cells are called s _ _ _ cells.
kidTest.explain: Stem cells can grow into every kind of blood cell.

advancedTest.q: Why does GVHD still occur after fully HLA-matched sibling transplants?
choices: Siblings carry mismatched ABO blood groups
Conditioning converts host HLA to donor HLA
Matched grafts lack regulatory T cells
advancedTest.explain: Polymorphic peptides presented by matched HLA can still be recognized by donor T cells. ABO mismatch does not drive GVHD.

advancedTest.q: Post-transplant cyclophosphamide limits GVHD while sparing regulatory T cells because:
choices: Tregs divide faster than effector cells
Tregs are removed before the infusion
advancedTest.explain: Proliferating alloreactive T cells are killed, while Tregs detoxify cyclophosphamide through high aldehyde dehydrogenase levels.

advancedTest.q: Which observation most directly showed that donor T cells mediate an anti-leukemia effect?
advancedTest.explain: Identical-twin grafts lack alloreactivity, and their higher relapse rate implicates allogeneic immunity in tumor control.

advancedTest.q: A transplant patient has diarrhea at day 30. Why is biopsy and testing important before escalating immunosuppression?
choices: Gut GVHD typically starts after day 100
Steroids are ineffective in gut GVHD
GVHD is ruled out by normal bilirubin
CMV colitis or C. difficile can mimic GVHD
advancedTest.explain: Infections and drug toxicity mimic gut GVHD, and extra immunosuppression would worsen an infection.

lessons.title: Lab-Grown Red Cells, Blood Substitutes & Pathogen Reduction

levels.kid:
Every day, people in hospitals need blood. Right now, all of that blood comes from kind people who donate it. But sometimes there isn't enough, and blood only stays fresh for a few weeks.

Scientists are working on three big ideas. First, they are growing red blood cells in the lab, starting from special "starter" cells, a bit like growing plants from seeds. Second, they are trying to make fake blood that can carry oxygen. That has been very hard, and some tries caused problems. Third, they are cleaning donated blood with special light that breaks the germs' instructions so the germs can't multiply, like scrambling a recipe so nobody can cook from it.

All three ideas aim to make blood safer and easier to get.
levels.hs:
Transfusion depends on volunteer donors, and that creates problems: shortages, short shelf life (red cells last about 42 days refrigerated, platelets only about 5 to 7 days at room temperature), rare blood types that are hard to match, and a small risk of passing on infections. Researchers are attacking these problems in three ways.

- **Lab-grown (cultured) red cells**: Scientists take **hematopoietic stem cells**, the cells that normally make blood in the bone marrow, and coax them in the lab to become mature red cells. In the UK **RESTORE trial**, healthy volunteers received small amounts of lab-grown red cells. It was the first trial to compare them with standard donated cells in the same person.
- **Blood substitutes**: These are oxygen carriers that are not real cells. **Hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers (HBOCs)** use free hemoglobin taken out of red cells. **Perfluorocarbons** are chemicals that dissolve lots of oxygen. Several HBOCs failed in trials because of side effects like high blood pressure and heart attacks.
- **Pathogen reduction**: Donated platelets and plasma can be treated with chemicals plus light that damage the DNA or RNA of viruses, bacteria and parasites. This stops them from copying themselves.

Example: The **INTERCEPT** system uses a chemical called **amotosalen** plus ultraviolet A light to treat platelets. This lowers the risk of bacterial infection, the most common infection from platelet transfusions.
levels.college:
**Cultured red blood cells (cRBCs).** Production mimics **erythropoiesis** (red cell production) in three phases. First, cells expand. Then they mature under **erythropoietin (EPO)**, stem cell factor and other factors. Finally the nucleus is pushed out (**enucleation**) to give reticulocytes. Cell sources include:
- **CD34+ cells** from peripheral blood or cord blood
- **Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs)**, which are adult cells reprogrammed into a stem-cell state; they enucleate poorly
- **Immortalized erythroid lines** such as BEL-A (Bristol), which can be grown in very large numbers

The RESTORE trial (NHS Blood and Transplant with Bristol and Cambridge) gave volunteers tiny amounts of cRBCs labeled with radioactive chromium and compared how long they survived against standard cells. Because a culture holds cells of a single age, cRBCs should live longer than donated blood, which is a mix of young and old cells. Longer survival could mean fewer transfusions for chronically transfused patients, for example in sickle cell disease.

**Oxygen therapeutics.**
- **HBOCs**: cell-free hemoglobin is cross-linked or polymerized, because free tetramers split into dimers that the kidneys filter out. Examples are bovine **HBOC-201 (Hemopure)** and human **PolyHeme**.
- **Perfluorocarbon (PFC) emulsions**: oxygen dissolves in them in direct proportion to its pressure, so patients need high inspired oxygen. **Fluosol-DA** was briefly approved by the FDA in 1989, then withdrawn.

**Pathogen reduction technologies (PRT).**
- **Amotosalen + UVA (INTERCEPT)**: a psoralen that slips between DNA/RNA strands and cross-links them; used for platelets and plasma.
- **Riboflavin + UV (Mirasol)**: damages nucleic acids, including by oxidizing guanine.
- **UVC alone (THERAFLEX)** and **solvent/detergent plasma**, which only kills viruses wrapped in a lipid envelope.

PRT also inactivates donor **T cells**, so it can replace irradiation for preventing transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease.
levels.phd:
**cRBC manufacture.** The biology is solved; the bottleneck is quantity. One unit holds about 2 x 10^12 red cells, and an adult makes about 2 x 10^11 a day. Static culture flasks can't reach that scale, so stirred-tank and perfusion bioreactors with high cell density are under development. The immortalized BEL-A line, made with inducible HPV16 E6/E7 by Trakarnsanga and colleagues (2017), solved the problem of limited supply. Remaining problems are incomplete enucleation, leftover nucleated precursors that must be removed, and the cost of recombinant cytokines. iPSC-derived cells tend to express embryonic and fetal globins (ε, γ) instead of adult β-globin, which raises their oxygen affinity. Gene editing also makes "universal" or rare-phenotype cells possible, for example knocking out antigens such as Kell, Duffy and RhD in BEL-A cells.

**Why HBOCs failed.** Free hemoglobin in plasma leaks out of blood vessels and binds **nitric oxide (NO)** very fast (about 10^7 M^-1 s^-1). Inside a red cell this binding is slowed by an unstirred layer around the cell and by the cell-free zone near the vessel wall. Losing NO causes vasoconstriction, high blood pressure and gut dysmotility. Autoxidation to methemoglobin and heme-driven oxidative stress add to the harm. Natanson's 2008 *JAMA* meta-analysis of 16 trials (3,711 patients) found HBOCs raised death (RR about 1.30) and heart attack (RR about 2.71). That largely halted Western development. The NO mechanism is still argued over: newer designs that oxygenate tissues less aggressively (MP4OX) still did not show benefit.

**PRT mechanisms.** Amotosalen intercalates into nucleic acid, then forms monoadducts and interstrand cross-links when hit with UVA (320-400 nm), blocking replication and transcription. Platelets and plasma have no nucleus, so the proteins they need survive. Treatment does reduce platelet count increments (corrected count increment, CCI), as shown in the SPRINT and EFFIPAP trials, though bleeding outcomes were largely similar. Red cells absorb UV light, so they need different chemistry: **amustaline (S-303)** with glutathione, which works without light. It is being tested in the ReCePI and RedeS trials.
levels.expert:
**Clinical positioning.** The first likely use for cRBCs is not general supply. It is patients whose phenotype is rare or who are **alloimmunized** against many antigens (some sickle cell patients, people with Bombay or Rh-null phenotypes), for whom compatible donors barely exist. Longer cRBC survival could cut transfusion frequency and iron loading. Regulators treat cRBCs as advanced therapy medicinal products, so they need potency assays for **deformability** (ektacytometry), 2,3-DPG content, ATP and in vivo recovery (the FDA expects at least 75% at 24 hours for stored red cells). Whether mass production can ever match donor blood on cost is still an open question.

**Oxygen carriers today.** In the US, HBOC-201 is mainly available through FDA **expanded access** for patients with life-threatening anemia who decline transfusion, such as Jehovah's Witnesses. Newer approaches include:
- **ErythroMer**, a lipid-encapsulated nanocell with controllable oxygen affinity
- Polymerized hemoglobins with low oxygen affinity
- Marine worm hemoglobin (**M101/HEMO2life**), used to preserve organs and grafts during transplantation

Defense-funded programs focus on blood substitutes for the field, where battle injuries occur far from blood banks.

**PRT in practice.**
- PRT platelets can be stored up to 7 days and can replace bacterial culture under FDA guidance (2019, updated 2020).
- They reduce transmission of emerging threats such as Zika, dengue and chikungunya, and lower the need for donor deferral.
- PRT does not reliably inactivate non-enveloped viruses like **hepatitis E** or parvovirus B19, bacterial spores, or prions.
- **Neurosurgical pitfall**: lower CCI means a post-transfusion count may look disappointing even when hemostasis is adequate. Interpret counts in light of the product type, and be aware that some centers keep conventional platelets for some intracranial bleeding.
- Cases of acute respiratory distress syndrome reported with PRT platelets in early studies were not confirmed in later pooled analyses.

**Whole blood PRT** (riboflavin, Mirasol) is attractive in places like sub-Saharan Africa where malaria is common: the AIMS trial in Ghana showed fewer *Plasmodium* transmissions. Open questions remain about red cell storage after treatment, neoantigen formation (amustaline antibodies triggered a redesign of the process), and cost-effectiveness in high-resource systems with low residual risk.

keyPoints: Cultured red cells are made from CD34+ cells, iPSCs or immortalized lines like BEL-A
RESTORE was the first trial to compare lab-grown red cells with standard donated cells in the same people
Scaling to about 2 trillion cells per unit is the main manufacturing barrier
HBOCs failed largely because free hemoglobin scavenges nitric oxide
Pathogen reduction (e.g., amotosalen + UVA) damages microbial DNA/RNA
Pathogen-reduced platelets lower bacterial risk and prevent TA-GVHD

test.q: Which cell source is used to grow red cells in the lab?
test.explain: CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells can be differentiated into red cells. The other options are mature cells that cannot become red cells.

test.q: Why should lab-grown red cells survive longer than donated red cells?
choices: They share a similar young age
They are coated in synthetic polymers
They keep their nucleus for repair
test.explain: A culture produces cells of a single age, while donated blood contains a mix of young and old cells.

test.q: What was the RESTORE trial's main goal?
choices: Comparing lab-grown and donated cell survival
Treating sickle cell disease with iPSCs
Licensing amotosalen for red cell units
test.explain: RESTORE compared the survival of lab-grown red cells with standard donated cells in healthy volunteers.

test.q: A major reason hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers failed was:
choices: Binding of nitric oxide causing vasoconstriction
Rapid antibody destruction by the spleen
Inability to carry any useful oxygen
test.explain: Free hemoglobin scavenges nitric oxide, leading to high blood pressure and heart attacks.

test.q: Why are cell-free hemoglobins cross-linked or polymerized?
choices: To make them taste less bitter
To let them form new red cell membranes
To stop dimers being filtered by kidneys
To raise their oxygen affinity sharply
test.explain: Free tetramers split into dimers that the kidneys filter out; cross-linking holds them together.

test.q: Perfluorocarbon emulsions carry oxygen by:
choices: Dissolving it in proportion to pressure
Binding it to an iron-heme core
test.explain: Oxygen dissolves physically in PFCs, so patients need high inspired oxygen levels.

test.q: How does amotosalen with UVA light inactivate pathogens?
choices: It cross-links their DNA or RNA
test.explain: Amotosalen intercalates into nucleic acids and cross-links them when exposed to UVA, so pathogens cannot replicate. Lipid-envelope disruption is how solvent/detergent plasma works.

test.q: Solvent/detergent plasma kills which pathogens?
test.explain: Solvents and detergents break lipid envelopes, so viruses without an envelope are not affected.

test.q: Pathogen reduction can replace irradiation because it:
test.explain: Inactivating donor T cells prevents transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease.

test.q: Pushing out the nucleus to form a reticulocyte is called ___.
test.explain: Enucleation is the final step of red cell maturation, and it is often incomplete in culture.

test.q: What is the name of the pathogen reduction system that uses amotosalen and UVA?
test.explain: INTERCEPT treats platelets and plasma.

test.q: What hormone drives red cell maturation in culture?
test.explain: EPO is a key growth factor in erythropoiesis.

kidTest.q: Where does all transfused blood come from today?
kidTest.explain: Kind people donate the blood used in hospitals.

kidTest.q: How do scientists grow red cells in a lab?
kidTest.explain: Special starter (stem) cells are coaxed into becoming red cells.

kidTest.q: What does special light do to germs in blood?
choices: Makes them glow in the dark
kidTest.explain: The light breaks the germs' instructions so they can't multiply.

kidTest.q: Why is fake blood hard to make?
kidTest.explain: Some early fake bloods caused harmful side effects.

kidTest.q: Red blood cells carry o _ _ _ _ _ around the body.
kidTest.explain: Red cells, and blood substitutes, are meant to carry oxygen.

advancedTest.q: Why does free hemoglobin scavenge NO far more than hemoglobin inside red cells?
choices: Nitric oxide diffuses poorly through blood plasma
Free hemoglobin holds more heme iron per molecule
It loses the diffusion barriers around red cells
Red cell hemoglobin is mostly oxidized methemoglobin
advancedTest.explain: Inside red cells, the unstirred layer and cell-free zone slow NO binding. Free hemoglobin that leaks out of vessels loses those barriers and binds NO quickly.

advancedTest.q: After a PRT platelet transfusion, a neurosurgical patient's platelet count rises less than expected but bleeding is controlled. The best interpretation is:
choices: Lower CCI is expected and hemostasis may be adequate
The patient likely has anti-platelet antibodies
The product was contaminated with bacteria
advancedTest.explain: Pathogen-reduced platelets give lower count increments, yet bleeding outcomes in trials were largely similar to standard platelets.

advancedTest.q: Why do red cell units need amustaline rather than amotosalen + UVA?
choices: Red cells contain nuclei that resist psoralens
Amotosalen is too large to enter plasma
Red cells absorb UV light, blocking photoactivation
Red cell units contain no pathogens
advancedTest.explain: Hemoglobin absorbs light, so red cells need chemistry that works without photoactivation.

advancedTest.q: iPSC-derived red cells expressing γ-globin would most likely show:
choices: Identical oxygen behavior to adult cells
Lower oxygen affinity than adult cells
Higher oxygen affinity than adult cells
advancedTest.explain: Fetal hemoglobin binds oxygen more tightly than adult hemoglobin, which changes how readily the cells release oxygen to tissues.
